question: Which component of the filtration barrier provides both size-selective and charge-selective restriction of circulating macromolecules?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss various presentations of glomerular diseases

options.rationale: The glomerular basement membrane contains type IV collagen and carries a negative charge, providing both size and charge selectivity.

The endothelium is part of the filtration barrier, but the described dual size and charge selectivity is attributed to the basement membrane. Endothelial injury would instead support a nephritic presentation.
Podocyte foot processes and slit diaphragms form another barrier component. Diffuse effacement would make this option relevant in minimal change disease.
The mesangial matrix supports the glomerulus but is not the filtration layer responsible for the stated dual selectivity. Mesangial expansion would fit disorders such as diabetic nephropathy.
The capsular epithelium is not one of the three specified components of the glomerular filter. Crescent formation involving the capsular space would make this structure clinically relevant.

question: Which urinary finding most strongly supports a predominantly inflammatory glomerular process rather than massive permeability-associated protein loss?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss various presentations of glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Oval fat bodies are associated with the lipid-rich sediment of nephrotic syndrome. They would be expected with massive proteinuria and a foamy urine appearance.
Red blood cell casts indicate glomerular bleeding and support nephritic injury involving endothelial inflammation.
Fatty casts support nephrotic syndrome rather than inflammatory glomerular bleeding. They would fit a presentation dominated by proteinuria above 3.5 g/day.
Urinary lipid findings are characteristic of nephrotic loss rather than nephritic inflammation. Marked proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia would make this finding appropriate.
Abundant lipid-containing elements point toward nephrotic syndrome. Dysmorphic erythrocytes or erythrocyte casts would instead support the process in the stem.

question: Which electron microscopic alteration characterizes minimal change disease?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Subepithelial humps characterize post-infectious glomerulonephritis. A delayed nephritic syndrome with low C3 would make this finding appropriate.
Basket-weave glomerular basement membrane alteration is associated with later Alport syndrome. Hearing or ocular abnormalities would support that finding.
Minimal change disease produces extensive podocyte foot process effacement despite little or no glomerular abnormality by light microscopy.
Random nonbranching fibrils measuring 10-12 nm characterize amyloid deposition. Congo red positivity would make this option correct.
Subendothelial deposits may occur in lupus nephritis rather than minimal change disease. Full-house immunofluorescence would support that process.

question: Which immunofluorescence pattern characterizes antibody-mediated injury directed against the glomerular filtration membrane?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Mesangial IgA deposition defines IgA nephropathy. Recurrent hematuria within 1-3 days of an upper respiratory infection would support this pattern.
Irregular capillary wall and mesangial C3 staining is associated with post-infectious glomerulonephritis. A preceding infection and depressed C3 would support it.
Full-house staining is a diagnostic feature of lupus nephritis. Systemic lupus with active urinary sediment would make this option appropriate.
Anti-GBM antibodies bind along the glomerular basement membrane, producing linear IgG staining.
Minimal immunoglobulin staining defines pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis. ANCA-associated vasculitis would support this pattern.

question: A renal specimen has sclerosis in fewer than half of sampled glomeruli, and each affected glomerulus has involvement of only part of its tuft. Which morphologic designation is most accurate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Diffuse global disease would involve at least half of glomeruli and the entire tuft of affected glomeruli. Those findings are absent here.
Focal involvement fits the proportion of glomeruli, but global sclerosis would involve the entire affected tuft. Complete tuft involvement would make this correct.
Segmental involvement fits each affected tuft, but diffuse disease would involve at least half of sampled glomeruli. That distribution is not present.
Mesangial proliferation describes increased mesangial cells and matrix rather than the specified distribution of sclerosis. Those proliferative findings would make this appropriate.
Focal indicates involvement of fewer than 50% of glomeruli, while segmental indicates involvement of only part of an affected tuft.

question: A child develops rapid-onset periorbital edema and heavy urinary protein loss. Serum creatinine is normal, and there is no hematuria or hypertension. Which initial approach is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: This typical childhood nephrotic presentation supports minimal change disease, which is usually treated empirically with corticosteroids without initial biopsy.
Initial biopsy is usually avoided in a typical childhood presentation. Hematuria, hypertension, abnormal creatinine, or steroid resistance after eight weeks would make biopsy appropriate.
Plasmapheresis is part of treatment for anti-GBM disease, not uncomplicated childhood nephrotic syndrome. Pulmonary hemorrhage with rapidly progressive renal failure would support it.
Combination antiretroviral therapy is central to HIV-associated nephropathy. HIV infection with high viral load and rapidly progressive kidney disease would make it appropriate.

Typical minimal change disease is treated with corticosteroids and has a high response rate in children. Observation would fit a self-limited childhood IgA vasculitis without significant renal disease.

question: A glomerulus is normal by routine light microscopy, while electron microscopy shows widespread alteration of the epithelial filtration surface. Which clinical pattern should accompany these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Hematuria with impaired filtration supports nephritic endothelial injury. Red blood cell casts and reduced GFR would make this pattern appropriate.
Minimal change disease alters podocyte foot processes and produces nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and usually normal creatinine.
Pulmonary hemorrhage with rapidly declining renal function suggests a pulmonary-renal syndrome. Linear IgG or pauci-immune findings would support that presentation.
This pairing supports Alport syndrome caused by abnormal type IV collagen. A basket-weave basement membrane would make it appropriate.
Purpura and abdominal pain support systemic IgA vasculitis. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposition would make this pattern correct.

question: A young adult has recurrent visible urinary discoloration beginning two days after upper respiratory infections. Which renal finding best unifies the timing and presentation?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Linear IgG deposition indicates anti-GBM disease. Rapid renal decline with pulmonary hemorrhage would make this finding appropriate.
Subepithelial humps support post-infectious glomerulonephritis, which follows infection after a longer latent period. A 10-14 day delay after pharyngitis would support it.
IgA nephropathy causes recurrent synpharyngitic hematuria within 1-3 days of infection and is defined by mesangial IgA deposits.
Diffuse foot process effacement is characteristic of minimal change disease. Rapid edema with nephrotic protein loss would make this finding appropriate.
Random nonbranching fibrils indicate renal amyloidosis. Congo red staining with apple-green birefringence would support that diagnosis.

question: A proliferative glomerular disorder shows increased mesangial matrix with interposition of cellular elements between newly formed membrane layers. Which light microscopic appearance should result?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Thin delicate capillary walls may be seen in minimal change disease. Normal light microscopy with podocyte effacement would support that diagnosis.
Global tuft collapse is associated with collapsing FSGS, including classic HIV-associated nephropathy. High viral load and large echogenic kidneys would support it.
Nodular mesangial sclerosis describes Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules in diabetic nephropathy. Prominent nodular expansion would make this correct.
Basement membrane duplication with cellular interposition produces the double-contour or tram-track appearance of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.
Extensive crescents characterize rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. A rapid loss of at least 50% of kidney function would support this pattern.

question: A renal specimen shows thick capillary walls without hypercellularity, granular capillary IgG staining, and external electron-dense deposits. Which diagnosis best matches this combination?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Minimal change disease has little light microscopic alteration and diffuse foot process effacement rather than granular deposits. Those findings would make it correct.
FSGS shows focal and segmental sclerosis rather than diffuse capillary-wall immune deposits. Sclerosis in fewer than half of glomeruli would support it.
MPGN produces hypercellular lobulated glomeruli and double-contour basement membranes. Those proliferative changes would make it correct.
Post-infectious disease shows endocapillary hypercellularity, neutrophils, and hump-like deposits. A delayed nephritic presentation with low C3 would support it.
Membranous nephropathy produces thick capillary walls, granular capillary-wall IgG, subepithelial deposits, and spike-and-dome remodeling.

question: A pathologist observes orange-red glomerular material that becomes apple-green under polarized light. Which ultrastructural finding should accompany this material?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Congo red positivity with apple-green birefringence identifies amyloid, which appears as randomly arranged nonbranching fibrils measuring 10-12 nm.
Foot process effacement characterizes minimal change disease and may also occur in HIV-associated FSGS. Normal light microscopy would support minimal change disease.
Subepithelial humps characterize post-infectious glomerulonephritis. A recent infection with depressed C3 would make this finding appropriate.
Lamellation and basket-weave change characterize later Alport syndrome. Hematuria with deafness or anterior lenticonus would support this finding.
Tubuloreticular aggregates are associated with lupus nephritis and classic HIV-associated nephropathy. Corresponding clinical and immunofluorescence findings would be required.

question: A glomerular disorder produces persistent microscopic hematuria, little protein loss, normal filtration, and no extrarenal abnormalities. Electron microscopy shows uniform membrane attenuation. Which expected course is most consistent?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Rapid progression would conflict with thin basement membrane disease. Crescentic glomerulonephritis with a rapid functional decline would support this course.
Thin basement membrane disease generally has a benign course, excellent prognosis, and requires no specific treatment.
Pulmonary hemorrhage is associated with pulmonary-renal syndromes rather than isolated thin basement membrane disease. Anti-GBM disease or ANCA vasculitis would support it.
Deafness and ocular abnormalities support Alport syndrome. Abnormal type IV collagen with basket-weave membranes would make this course appropriate.
Thrombosis and severe edema are complications of nephrotic syndrome, especially membranous nephropathy. Heavy proteinuria would be required.

question: A glomerular biopsy shows necrosis and crescents at varying stages with absent or minimal deposits on immunofluorescence and electron microscopy. Which pathogenic category is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Anti-GBM injury produces linear IgG staining rather than minimal immunofluorescence. Uniform-stage crescents and circulating anti-GBM antibodies would support it.
IgA-mediated disease produces mesangial IgA deposits. Recurrent synpharyngitic hematuria with mesangial staining would make it correct.
Pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis has necrosis and variably aged crescents with little or no staining or deposits.
Post-infectious injury produces granular C3 and immunoglobulin staining with subepithelial humps. Those deposits are absent here.
Lupus nephritis commonly produces full-house staining and mesangial or capillary deposits. Those immune deposits would make this option correct.

question: A patient has heavy protein loss and stable kidney function. Evaluation identifies a glomerular disease with the greatest stated risk of deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Which diagnosis is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss various presentations of glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Minimal change disease causes nephrotic syndrome but is not identified as having the greatest thromboembolic risk. Normal microscopy with foot process effacement would support it.
IgA nephropathy usually presents with hematuria rather than the highest thromboembolic risk. Mesangial IgA deposition would support that diagnosis.
Post-infectious disease produces a nephritic presentation with low C3. A delayed onset after infection would support it.
Membranous nephropathy is specifically associated with the highest risk of deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism from nephrotic hypercoagulability.
Thin basement membrane disease causes isolated microscopic hematuria, with proteinuria being uncommon. A benign hematuric course would support it.

question: A child develops palpable lower-extremity lesions, abdominal pain, joint discomfort, proteinuria, and microscopic hematuria. Which tissue finding would most directly confirm the systemic process?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Linear renal IgG suggests anti-GBM disease. Pulmonary hemorrhage with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis would make this finding appropriate.
Subepithelial humps indicate post-infectious glomerulonephritis. A delayed nephritic syndrome with low C3 would support that finding.
Pauci-immune crescents support ANCA-associated vasculitis. Pulmonary-renal disease with minimal immunoglobulin staining would make this appropriate.
Basket-weave glomerular membranes support Alport syndrome. Deafness and ocular abnormalities would make that finding appropriate.
The presentation supports IgA vasculitis, and skin biopsy demonstrates leukocytoclastic vasculitis with heavy IgA and complement deposition.

question: A 7-year-old boy develops edema and heavy urinary protein loss. Creatinine is normal, and blood pressure is not elevated. After eight weeks of corticosteroids, protein loss persists. Which next step is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Steroid resistance after eight weeks is an atypical feature in childhood nephrotic syndrome and is an indication for renal biopsy.
Persistent proteinuria after the specified steroid trial requires further evaluation. Observation would better fit self-limited childhood IgA vasculitis without progressive renal findings.
Plasma exchange is used for anti-GBM disease rather than isolated steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome. Hemoptysis and rapid renal decline would support it.
Antiretroviral therapy treats HIV-associated nephropathy. HIV infection with high viral load and low CD4 count would make it appropriate.
Antibiotics are given in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. A preceding streptococcal infection with low C3 and nephritic sediment would support this treatment.

question: A 29-year-old man has recurrent visible urinary discoloration beginning one day after sore throats. Urinalysis between episodes shows microscopic blood and mild protein loss. Which treatment best addresses long-term renal risk?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: This regimen is used with intravenous steroids for anti-GBM disease. Pulmonary hemorrhage and rapidly progressive renal decline would make it appropriate.
The timing supports IgA nephropathy, for which RAAS blockade lowers blood pressure, reduces proteinuria, and slows renal progression.
Routine immediate high-dose steroid monotherapy is not the stated foundational treatment for this presentation. Severe lupus nephritis requires high-dose steroid plus another immunosuppressive agent.
Combination antiretroviral therapy treats HIV-associated nephropathy. HIV infection with high viral load and large echogenic kidneys would make it appropriate.
Antibiotic treatment of patients and cohabitants is recommended for post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. A longer postinfectious latency would support that approach.

question: A 34-year-old patient has rapidly worsening kidney function, hemoptysis, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Renal immunofluorescence shows a continuous IgG pattern along capillary walls. Which treatment is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Antibiotics address post-streptococcal infection but do not remove pathogenic anti-GBM antibodies. A delayed nephritic syndrome without pulmonary hemorrhage would fit that approach.
RAAS blockade and salt restriction are supportive measures for proteinuric disease but are insufficient for severe anti-GBM pulmonary-renal syndrome.
The presentation and linear IgG pattern indicate Goodpasture syndrome, treated with intravenous steroids, cyclophosphamide, and plasmapheresis.
Tacrolimus may be used in steroid-resistant FSGS. A nephrotic presentation with focal segmental sclerosis would make this regimen relevant.
Observation is unsafe in rapidly progressive anti-GBM disease. Stable membranous nephropathy with limited proteinuria might instead be observed.

question: A 46-year-old patient has hemoptysis, rapidly declining renal function, chronic sinus pain, and bloody nasal drainage. Kidney biopsy shows crescentic injury with little immune staining. Which serologic pattern is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: P-ANCA targeting myeloperoxidase is more typical of microscopic polyangiitis. Lack of upper respiratory involvement and granulomatous inflammation would support it.
Anti-GBM antibodies target the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen and produce linear staining. The pauci-immune biopsy and upper airway disease argue against this pattern.
IgA nephropathy is defined by mesangial IgA deposits rather than the described pauci-immune pulmonary-renal syndrome. Synpharyngitic hematuria would support it.
Upper airway disease, pulmonary hemorrhage, and pauci-immune crescentic nephritis indicate granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which is strongly associated with C-ANCA targeting PR3.
Full-house immunofluorescence supports lupus nephritis rather than pauci-immune vasculitis. Systemic lupus findings and immune deposits would make this pattern appropriate.

question: A 52-year-old patient has hemoptysis and rapidly progressive renal failure but no sinus, nasal, or upper airway disease. Biopsy shows necrotizing small-vessel inflammation without granulomas and minimal immune deposits. Which diagnosis is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis typically includes granulomatous inflammation and upper respiratory tract involvement. Those findings would make this diagnosis correct.
Anti-GBM disease produces linear glomerular IgG staining rather than pauci-immune injury. Linear staining and circulating antibodies would support it.
Lupus nephritis has immune deposits and full-house staining. Those findings are absent in this pauci-immune process.
Post-infectious disease produces granular immune deposits and often low C3. A preceding infection with subepithelial humps would support it.
Microscopic polyangiitis causes pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis without granulomatous inflammation or upper airway involvement.

question: A 9-year-old girl develops edema, cola-colored urine, hypertension, and erythrocyte casts two weeks after pharyngitis. Serum C3 is decreased while C4 is normal. Which management is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: The latency, nephritic syndrome, and complement pattern support post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Treatment is supportive, with antibiotics given for the streptococcal infection.
Plasmapheresis and steroids are components of anti-GBM treatment. Pulmonary hemorrhage with linear glomerular IgG would support that approach.
Immunosuppression has no stated role in post-streptococcal disease, even with crescents. Severe lupus nephritis would support this combination.
Tacrolimus may be used for steroid-resistant FSGS. Focal segmental sclerosis with persistent nephrotic proteinuria would make it appropriate.
Supportive renal care is appropriate, but antibiotic therapy should be given to affected patients and their cohabitants. Absence of suspected streptococcal infection would remove that indication.

question: A 41-year-old patient has edema and urinary protein excretion of 5.2 g/day [less than 3.5 g/day]. Biopsy shows thick capillary walls, granular IgG, and subepithelial deposits. Which complication requires particular vigilance?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Pulmonary granulomatous inflammation is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Upper airway disease and pauci-immune nephritis would make this complication relevant.
The pathology indicates membranous nephropathy, which carries the highest stated risk of deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
Sensorineural deafness is associated with Alport syndrome. Persistent hematuria and basket-weave basement membranes would support it.
Synpharyngitic hematuria is characteristic of IgA nephropathy. Mesangial IgA deposition would make this finding appropriate.
Palpable purpura is characteristic of IgA vasculitis. Abdominal pain, arthralgia, and skin IgA deposits would support it.

question: A 33-year-old man with untreated HIV has heavy proteinuria, rapidly progressive chronic kidney disease, relatively little edema, and normal blood pressure. Ultrasonography shows enlarged echogenic kidneys. Which renal lesion is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Diffuse capillary-wall thickening with subepithelial deposits indicates membranous nephropathy. Granular IgG and spike formation would support it.
Mesangial IgA injury characterizes IgA nephropathy. Recurrent hematuria shortly after respiratory infections would support it.
The presentation is classic for HIV-associated nephropathy, which is associated with the collapsing variant of FSGS.
Post-infectious disease causes an acute nephritic syndrome with low C3. A recent infection and subepithelial humps would support it.
Thin basement membrane disease causes isolated microscopic hematuria with little proteinuria and a benign course. Those features conflict with this case.

question: A patient with the renal presentation described has a high viral load and CD4 count of 110 cells/µL. Which intervention most directly improves the driving disease process and may permit renal recovery?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Steroids alone do not address the direct viral contribution to HIV-associated nephropathy. Typical minimal change disease would be treated initially with steroids.
This combination is used with steroids for anti-GBM disease. Pulmonary hemorrhage and linear IgG staining would support it.
Antibiotics for patients and cohabitants are recommended in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. A recent streptococcal infection would make this appropriate.
All HIV-positive individuals should begin combination antiretroviral therapy at diagnosis. In HIV-associated nephropathy, it reduces proteinuria and progression risk and may allow renal recovery.
Untreated HIV-associated nephropathy can progress rapidly, so observation alone does not address the driving process. Stable membranous disease with limited proteinuria might be observed.

question: A 24-year-old man has lifelong microscopic hematuria, progressive proteinuria, declining renal function, hearing loss, and a cone-shaped anterior lens abnormality. Which ultrastructural finding is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Uniform thinning supports thin basement membrane disease, which lacks extrarenal manifestations and usually has a benign course. Those features are absent here.
Foot process effacement supports minimal change disease. Rapid edema with nephrotic proteinuria and normal creatinine would make it appropriate.
Subepithelial humps indicate post-infectious glomerulonephritis. A delayed acute nephritic syndrome after infection would support them.
Random nonbranching fibrils characterize amyloidosis. Congo red positivity and apple-green birefringence would support this finding.
Hematuria, progressive renal failure, sensorineural deafness, and anterior lenticonus identify Alport syndrome, which develops thin and thick basket-weave basement membranes.

question: A 30-year-old woman with systemic autoimmune disease develops hypertension, edema, rising creatinine, and urine containing erythrocytes, leukocytes, and multiple cellular casts. Which next step most directly guides prognosis and treatment intensity?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: The active telescoped sediment supports lupus nephritis. Renal biopsy identifies the class, severity, activity, and chronicity that direct management and predict outcome.
Serum IgA is neither sensitive nor specific even for IgA vasculitis. A skin or renal biopsy would confirm IgA deposition when confirmation is needed.
Rising creatinine and active sediment require classification because lupus classes have different prognoses and treatments. Observation fits less severe stable disease after assessment.
Open lung biopsy has high yield in granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not suspected lupus nephritis without pulmonary findings. Pulmonary-renal disease with upper airway involvement would support it.
Skin biopsy can confirm IgA vasculitis when purpura is present. It does not classify the renal lesion described in this patient.

question: Biopsy in a patient with systemic autoimmune disease shows active lesions in 65% of glomeruli. Immunofluorescence demonstrates diffuse deposition of multiple immunoglobulins and complement components. Which class is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Class III involves fewer than 50% of glomeruli. That threshold is exceeded in this specimen.
Class IV lupus nephritis involves at least 50% of glomeruli. Full-house staining supports lupus immune complex disease.
Class V has a membranous pattern with subepithelial deposits. Diffuse active proliferative involvement of 65% of glomeruli favors class IV.
Class VI requires more than 90% sclerotic glomeruli. The stem describes active immune complex lesions rather than advanced sclerosis.
Class II is mesangial proliferative lupus nephritis. Diffuse involvement beyond the mesangium would be required for class IV.

question: A 38-year-old patient has nephritic and nephrotic features with declining filtration. Biopsy shows enlarged lobulated hypercellular glomeruli and duplicated capillary walls. Which additional laboratory finding is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: MPGN is associated with low rather than increased C3. Increased C3 is not the stated complement pattern.
Anti-GBM antibodies indicate type I crescentic disease with linear staining. They do not explain the duplicated capillary walls described.
The pathology indicates MPGN, in which low serum C3 is common.
Serum IgA elevation is neither sensitive nor specific for IgA vasculitis and does not define MPGN. Mesangial IgA deposits would support IgA nephropathy.
Anti-PLA2R antibodies are associated with primary membranous nephropathy. Thick walls without hypercellularity would make that association relevant.

question: A 27-year-old patient has a 55% decline in kidney function over six weeks. Biopsy shows crescents in 70% of glomeruli, and immunofluorescence demonstrates granular immune deposits. Which pathogenic type is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Type I RPGN is anti-GBM-mediated and produces linear rather than granular staining. Anti-GBM antibodies would make this type correct.
Type III RPGN has absent or minimal immunoglobulin staining. ANCA association with little immune deposition would support it.
The rapid functional decline and extensive crescents define a rapidly progressive nephritic process rather than a noncrescentic nephrotic disorder.
Type II RPGN is immune complex-mediated and therefore produces granular localization of deposited immune complexes.
Hemodynamic injury does not account for granular immune deposits and widespread crescents. Hyperfiltration-associated secondary FSGS would support a hemodynamic mechanism.

question: A 6-year-old child has palpable purpura over the legs and buttocks, abdominal pain, arthralgia, and microscopic hematuria. Kidney function is stable, and symptoms are improving. Which management is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Plasma exchange is used for anti-GBM pulmonary-renal disease. Linear IgG staining with rapid renal decline would support it.
This intensive immunosuppression is used for severe lupus nephritis or anti-GBM disease with additional therapy. Stable self-limited IgA vasculitis does not require it.
Calcineurin inhibitors may be used in steroid-resistant FSGS or selected membranous disease. Those diagnoses are not supported by this systemic presentation.
Combination antiretroviral therapy treats HIV-associated nephropathy. HIV infection with high viral load and collapsing FSGS would support it.
Childhood IgA vasculitis is generally self-limited and resolves without specific therapy when renal involvement is mild and stable.

question: A 63-year-old patient has nephrotic protein loss and biopsy-confirmed primary membranous disease. Protein excretion is limited, and serum creatinine remains stable. Which initial strategy is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss clinical aspects and pathological features of common glomerular diseases

options.rationale: Membranous nephropathy with less proteinuria and stable creatinine may be observed while receiving supportive therapy such as RAAS blockade, blood pressure management, and appropriate thrombosis prophylaxis.
Plasma exchange removes pathogenic antibodies in anti-GBM disease. Pulmonary hemorrhage and linear IgG staining would support it.
Cyclophosphamide may be paired with steroids for definitive treatment in selected membranous disease, but stable limited disease can initially be observed.
Antiretroviral therapy is indicated for HIV-associated nephropathy. Untreated HIV with collapsing FSGS would make it appropriate.
Antibiotic treatment of cohabitants is associated with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. A preceding streptococcal infection would be required.
